title: The Small Songbook
premise: After a catastrophic final performance leaves cellist Mirabel Underhill with a shattered reputation and a vow to keep her heart 'trained and contained,' she retreats to a derelict orchard cottage on Saltrow Island, only to discover the deed bears two names: hers and that of Jonah Vane, the estranged childhood friend whose testimony once destroyed her family. Neither will leave, so they strike a bitter bargain to share the property until the last ferry of the season, when one of them must buy the other out. As they restore the dying orchard together, Mirabel uncovers letters proving Jonah lied under pressure from her own father, forcing her to confront that her memory of betrayal was itself a survival story she told herself. In the end, Mirabel chooses justice over vengeance—publicly clearing Jonah's name at the cost of her father's posthumous reputation—and boards the last ferry not to flee but to return, having signed the deed over to both of them.
about_author: Rosalind Blackwood is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing her own stories. She lives on a cold northern coast, where she keeps an untidy garden and an even more untidy notebook of things people confess to strangers on ferries.

chapters.title: The Tuning Silence
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Eight months after her disastrous final concert, Mirabel arrives at the Saltrow Island cottage she secretly inherited, rehearsing her mantra: the heart is a muscle, containable. She finds fresh footprints in the frost and a second name inked on the deed. Emotional beat: brittle control cracking into unease.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Deed
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah Vane, a burned-out luthier fleeing his own scandal, reveals he inherited half the orchard from Mirabel's late aunt—and he isn't leaving either. They agree to split the house until the season's final ferry, when one buys the other out. Emotional beat: hostile truce, mutual wariness masking old grief.

chapters.title: What the Orchard Remembers
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Clearing storm-felled trees, they unearth the aunt's ledger showing the orchard was kept alive for twenty years by anonymous payments—payments timed to the collapse of Mirabel's family. Mirabel begins questioning her tidy story of betrayal. Emotional beat: first hairline fracture in her certainty.

chapters.title: A Muscle Like Any Other
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. A week of forced cooperation: shared meals, repaired fences, Jonah fixing Mirabel's cracked cello without being asked. When she plays again for the first time, her hands shake and he pretends not to notice. Emotional beat: tenderness arriving uninvited; both fight it.

chapters.title: The Ferry Manifest
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A visiting journalist hunting the story behind Mirabel's ruined concert recognizes Jonah as the witness who testified against her family. He lies to protect her, then realizes protecting her means confronting what he actually said all those years ago. Emotional beat: guilt resurfacing; stakes rise beyond the island.

chapters.title: Letters in the Root Cellar
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel discovers a bundle of letters proving her father coerced Jonah's testimony to shield his own fraud—and that her aunt knew everything. Her entire architecture of grievance collapses. Emotional beat: devastation; the person in the mirror becomes the hardest one to forgive.

chapters.title: Storm Glass
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. A violent gale traps them in the cottage; the truth spills out between candle stubs—his coercion, her years of hatred built on a lie. They argue, weep, and nearly cross a line neither can take back. Emotional beat: raw catharsis; intimacy born of wreckage rather than comfort.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The journalist publishes anyway, twisting the story. Mirabel faces a choice: let the false narrative stand and keep her quiet life, or go public with her father's fraud and lose whatever protection his name still gives her. Emotional beat: resolve hardening; justice chosen over safety.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. On the dock before the final crossing, Mirabel publicly tells the whole truth to the islanders and the press, clearing Jonah and damning her father. Then she hands him the buyout check—signed over to both their names instead. Emotional beat: climax and release; love stated plainly, without armor.

chapters.title: Spring Pruning
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Months later, the orchard blooms again. Mirabel schedules a small comeback recital in the restored barn while Jonah builds her a new instrument from the storm-felled wood. Forgiveness, she learns, is daily work, like pruning. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope; the heart retrained, not contained.
